front.title: Homing Pigeon Message Protocol, Version 3: DTLS 1.3 via Email

abstract.t: This document specifies version 3 of the Homing Pigeon message protocol. Version 3 is a transport extension to version 1, not a replacement for it: every version 1 message keeps its meaning, the version 1 job acceptance gate is unchanged, and version 3 changes exactly one thing -- the carriage of the version 1 DTLS session profile.

Version 1 defines a DTLS 1.3 session profile: one cipher suite, a pre-shared key taken from the protocol's shared secret, ephemeral Diffie-Hellman on every handshake, and the platform_info disclosure carried in the server's EncryptedExtensions. Version 1 binds that profile to a live datagram path. This document binds the same profile to the email binding: handshake flights and protected records are carried as email messages over the store-and-forward mailbox, so a session can be opened by an email, completed over further emails, and then carry jobs and results inside it, with the perfect forward secrecy of the version 1 profile intact on a carrier that has no live path at all.

The objects carried inside the session remain version 1 objects: a job or a result inside a session is the version 1 object, unchanged, carrying the version value version 1 defines. The 3 of this document's title numbers this document and its carriage; it is not a value of any object's version field, and nothing in this document mints a version 3 object. HP-DTLS/3, the frame header this document defines, is a carriage label whose digit is the carriage generation, not a protocol version.
This document is a local, unsubmitted draft. It has not been posted to the Internet-Drafts directory, and it requests no IANA action.

section.name: Introduction
section.t: Version 1 is the base document. Its email binding is store-and-forward: a job object is an email, a result object is an email, and either can wait in a mailbox for as long as the mailbox keeps it. Version 1's DTLS binding is the opposite shape: a live session over datagrams, with handshake flights exchanged in seconds and records protected by keys that exist only for that session.

Each binding gives up what the other has. The email binding carries a job anywhere mail goes, including to a runner that is only ever reachable through a mailbox, but the object crypto of version 1 -- a signature and, by default, per-job encryption under the shared secret -- provides no forward secrecy: the shared secret is long-lived, and mail is stored. The DTLS binding provides forward secrecy, because its session keys are derived from an ephemeral exchange and erased with the session, but it needs a live path, and a runner behind a mailbox has none.

Version 3 carries the version 1 DTLS profile, unchanged, over the email binding. What it removes is the confidentiality side of the trade: a runner reachable only through a mailbox gains the session's forward secrecy. What it does not remove is the rest of the trade -- store-and- forward delay, a transcript stored at every hop, visible subjects and sizes, and a pre-authentication surface the size of the mailbox:

li.t: A DTLS handshake flight is carried as 1 or more email messages (Sections 5 and 6).
The receiver's mailbox parser recognizes a DTLS initialization flight and routes it to the DTLS engine, never to the job execution path (Section 8).
Once the session is established, jobs and results travel as application data inside it (Section 10), and each job still faces the version 1 acceptance gate in full (Section 10.2).

The platform disclosure rides the handshake on this carrier exactly as on the datagram binding, in EncryptedExtensions, so the initiator holds it when the session is established and no post-handshake poll of the mailbox is needed to learn it (Section 11).

section.t: Nothing else in version 1 changes. The deltas in this document are stated as deltas: where this document says a version 1 rule applies, it applies as written there.

The same profile therefore runs on 2 bindings, and their names are kept distinct. On the version 1 datagram binding it is DTLS, with no qualifier: the submitter is told the runner's IP address and port, and DTLS runs over UDP datagrams as defines. On this document's binding it is DTLS via email: the same profile's datagrams ride email messages, and no inbound UDP listener -- and no firewall hole for one -- is needed. A deployment MAY offer either binding, or both; the profile, the handshake, and the acceptance gate are the same on each.

section.name: Status of this document
section.t: This is a local working draft, revision -00, dated 2026-11-02. It is not an Internet-Draft of record: it has not been submitted to the IETF datatracker or posted to the Internet-Drafts directory, no submission is requested by this text, and the IANA considerations (Section 15) request no assignment. The carriage this document specifies is implemented and tested in the Homing Pigeon software suite under an opt-in configuration option; the option is off by default.

section.name: Requirements Language
section.t: The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 when, and only when, they appear in all capitals, as shown here.

section.name: Terminology
section.t: The terms of version 1 apply: the runner, the submitter, the shared secret, the job object, the result object, the acceptance gate, and the platform disclosure. This document adds:

dd.t: 1 email message carrying all or part of exactly 1 DTLS datagram under this carriage.

the identifier in a flight subject (Section 5.1) that names 1 mail-carried session attempt. It is a routing label chosen by the initiator. It is not a credential, not a DTLS identity, and not the mailbox's identifier for any message.
the set of flight mails that together carry 1 segmented datagram, named by a transfer identifier (Section 5.2).
the rules of Sections 5 to 9: how datagrams become flight mail, how flight mail becomes datagrams again, and how the mailbox parser dispatches each.

section.name: The DTLS Profile on This Carriage
The profile is version 1's, unchanged
section.t: The session profile of version 1 Sections 19 and 20 applies to this carriage without modification, except where a later section of this document states a delta explicitly. In particular:

li.t: DTLS 1.3 is the session protocol. The 1 cipher suite is TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384.

The pre-shared key is the shared secret of version 1. The shared secret is an authenticator and only an authenticator; it is never the session key, which is derived from the ephemeral exchange of every handshake. There is no second secret and no new key material in this document.

Only the psk_dhe_ke key exchange mode is used. psk_ke MUST NOT be offered, accepted, or fallen back to, in a full handshake or in resumption. Every handshake, full or resumed, carries a fresh ephemeral share -- X25519, or the hybrid share of Section 4.4 where that section applies. This is the rule the perfect forward secrecy property of Section 16.1 rests on, and this carriage does not relax it.
The responder is stateless until a HelloRetryRequest cookie validates, exactly as on the datagram binding.
Connection IDs are used in both directions.
Early data is not used; there is no 0-RTT on this carriage. A ClientHello that carries early data is a malformed flight on this carriage and MUST be rejected (Section 13).
The platform_info extension is offered empty in the ClientHello and, when offered, MAY be answered in EncryptedExtensions only, exactly as version 1 Section 20 states (Section 11 of this document).

section.t: Certificates are not part of this profile, in either direction: version 1 Section 19 says so of the profile, and the profile applies here without modification, so the exclusion covers this carriage as it covers the datagram binding. Nothing in this document adds a certificate path or any other authentication mechanism; the shared secret is the only credential the handshake knows, on this carriage as on the other. A ClientHello that offers no pre_shared_key extension is refused before any key is derived: there is no other credential for it to fall back to.
The UDP port 20220 of version 1 is a local default of the datagram binding. This carriage has no port: its addresses are mailboxes.

section.name: What the carriage changes, and what it does not
section.t: The carriage changes the unit of transport. DTLS is written for datagrams that arrive whole, in order or not, within seconds. Mail arrives whole per message, in no guaranteed order, after delays of seconds to days, sometimes more than once, and with a size limit far below a mailbox's own. Sections 5 to 9 exist to bridge exactly those differences -- size, ordering, duplication, delay -- and nothing else.

The carriage does not change the cryptography, the handshake, the record protection, the session's authentication, or the job acceptance gate -- with the single exception stated in Section 4.4, the hybrid ephemeral share, which changes what the ephemeral exchange is made of and nothing around it. An implementation MUST NOT use this carriage as a reason to alter any of those beyond that stated exception.

section.name: Enablement
section.t: This carriage is opt-in. A runner enables it by explicit configuration (in the reference implementation, the dtls_via_email option, which only the literal boolean true enables). A runner that has not enabled it treats flight mail as it treats any other mail its parser does not dispatch, and its existing secret boundary is unchanged: the shared secret is handed to the component that terminates DTLS only when the carriage is enabled, exactly as it is handed to the datagram binding's listener when that binding is enabled.

A submitter discovers the carriage the way it discovers the platform: by attempting it and reading the outcome, or from the platform card of a prior exchange. There is no negotiation message, and a failed attempt has no effect on the ordinary email binding, which continues to work exactly as before.

A platform card MAY state, as an unauthenticated fact, that the runner offers this carriage. The fact is trusted for nothing except whether an attempt is worth making. It grants nothing. Admission remains the handshake's and the acceptance gate's (Section 10.2).

section.name: The hybrid share
section.t: The one delta this document states against the profile of Section 4.1 concerns the ephemeral share itself. On this carriage, a client offers, beside the X25519 share, the hybrid share X25519MLKEM768 : in the client share, the ML-KEM-768 encapsulation key followed by an X25519 share; in the server share, the ML-KEM ciphertext followed by an X25519 share; and a shared secret that is the ML-KEM secret followed by the X25519 secret, fed into the same key schedule the X25519 secret feeds on the datagram binding. A responder on this carriage that is offered the hybrid share selects it. A responder that does not implement this section -- and every peer on the datagram binding, where the version 1 profile stands unchanged -- selects the X25519 share, and the session is an ordinary version 1 session. The hybrid rides under the same psk_dhe_ke rule: a fresh hybrid share in every handshake, full or resumed, the shared secret still only authenticating, and TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384 still the suite. The home of the group is this carriage's profile; the datagram binding does not offer it.

The responder MUST perform the encapsulation-key check of FIPS 203 Section 7.2 on a hybrid client share and MUST abort the handshake with an illegal_parameter alert when it fails, as requires. A hybrid share of any size other than the one fixes, and a hybrid session whose Finished does not verify, fail the handshake closed; nothing falls back to a weaker exchange in answer to a failure (Section 12).

What the hybrid buys is stated in Section 16.1: it narrows the recorded-session limit of the bare X25519 exchange. It changes nothing else in this document: not the gate, not the framing, not the disclosure, not the bounds.

section.name: The flight subject
section.t: Flight mail is recognized by its subject, under the subject grammar of version 1 (spelled out in the reference implementation in 1 place, so every reader routes the same subjects). The flight subject is:
In ABNF , with the separator set as version 1 defines it:
section.artwork: flight-subject = "[HOMING-PIGEON]" 1*gap "dtls" 1*gap session-id session-id = 1*128 session-id-char ; and not "." or ".." session-id-char = ALPHA / DIGIT / "." / "_" / "-"
section.t: The session-id alphabet is stated here in full and does not inherit version 1's word-char: it is an alphabet safe in a mail header field (, Section 2.2) and as a filesystem name, and a future widening of version 1's production MUST NOT widen it.

The mail session-id is chosen by the initiator, 1 per session attempt; a resumption attempt is a new attempt and takes a new mail session-id. The responder answers flight mail for an attempt under the same mail session-id it arrived under.

A mail user agent that replies to flight mail may prepend a reply prefix to its subject. A receiver MAY accept at most 1 leading "Re:" or "Fwd:" (case-insensitive), and only when the remainder is exactly a flight subject. A chain of prefixes, or any other text before the marker, is not a flight subject.

The prefixes are mail user agent convention, not subject syntax: the Subject field is unstructured, and Section 3.6.5 describes "Re:" as something a reply's field body may start with. The acceptance rule here is this carriage's own, stated so a receiver's tolerance is a decision of this document and not a claim about the message format.

Subjects route; they never authenticate. A receiver MUST NOT treat a flight subject, a mail session-id, or any mail header (From, To, Reply-To, Message-ID, the mailbox UID, or arrival order) as evidence of who sent a flight. Authentication is the DTLS handshake's, applied to the datagram after reassembly (Section 6), and to nothing else.

An implementation MAY also accept the unaddressed harness shape -- subject exactly [HOMING-PIGEON] dtls and a body that is the base64 of 1 datagram -- inside an in-process test harness that is not a mailbox. That shape carries no mail session-id, cannot be bound to a session under Section 9.2, and MUST NOT be required by any deployment. A deployment mailbox MUST NOT feed it to a DTLS stack. On that mailbox it is malformed flight mail (Section 8.3): consumed, dropped, and worth no answer.

section.name: The flight frame
section.t: The frame of a flight mail is carried in a dedicated MIME part of the message, whose content type is application/hp-dtls3 -- a name in the standards tree that no registration backs: this document is local and requests no media type registration for it (Section 15). The part's content, under Content-Transfer-Encoding base64, is 1 header line, 1 line break, and 1 base64 chunk:
section.artwork: HP-DTLS/3 transfer=<t> part=<i> parts=<n> bytes=<b> sha384=<d> <base64 chunk>
section.t: where:

li.t: t is the transfer identifier: 16 lowercase hexadecimal digits, chosen fresh by the sender for each datagram it sends under this carriage.
i and n are the 0-based index of this part and the total number of parts, in decimal. An unsegmented datagram is part 0 of 1.

b is the total length of the datagram in octets, in decimal. The field publishes the datagram's exact length, which is consistent while this document specifies no padding (Section 16.2); if padding is ever added, b is the padded length, or the field would undo the padding.
d is the SHA-384 digest of the whole datagram, as 96 lowercase hexadecimal digits.

the chunk is a slice of the base64 encoding ( Section 4, with padding) of the whole datagram. Slices are cut on base64 group boundaries, so each chunk decodes on its own and the decoded chunks, concatenated in index order, are the datagram exactly.

section.t: The digest binds the parts of a transfer to each other and to the datagram they claim to carry. It is not a signature and MUST NOT be treated as authentication: a receiver verifies it to know the datagram is whole, and authenticates the datagram afterwards, by DTLS.

The frame rides as its own part, and not as text in the message's text part, precisely so that what intermediate agents do to text cannot reach it: a mail gateway that appends a disclaimer or a banner to the text part -- the routine rewriting of real mail paths -- does not touch the flight. This is the dedicated-part practice records for the same reason. Text outside the part is not the frame and MUST be ignored for framing.

The part is a leaf part: a direct part of the message's multipart structure, not the content of a message/rfc822 part. A sender MUST NOT wrap it in one. A receiver finds the frame part by its content type wherever it sits in the part tree, and the wrapped shape is read where it is met -- but an intermediary that treats a message/rfc822 container as an opaque attachment can drop the flight with the container, and a sender has no reason to hand it the chance: the serialization this document pins is the leaf.

The header line is the part's 1st line. Base64 folding at 76 columns inside the part is accepted: the chunk is read with its whitespace removed. Quoted-printable MUST NOT be used for the part and MUST NOT be accepted for it: a part whose transfer encoding is not base64 carries no frame.

A message with no application/hp-dtls3 part is read in the naked shape this carriage began with: the frame as the 1st text/plain part's text, as a job body under version 1 is read, with no preamble and no trailer. When a typed part is present it is the only frame source: a frame-shaped text part does not rescue a typed part that does not frame, and a part that does not frame is malformed flight mail (Section 8.3).

The naked shape is read for senders that never used the typed part: a local harness, and senders that predate the part. It is not a 2nd copy of the frame. A sender that uses the typed part places the frame there and nowhere else; its text part carries at most a note for a human, and MUST NOT carry the frame. A receiver cannot tell that a typed part was removed on the way. It applies the rule it can check: no typed part means the naked shape, and a naked body that does not frame is malformed flight mail (Section 8.3). A conforming sender's text does not frame, so an intermediary that removes the typed part ends that flight. The flight is repaired, if at all, by the DTLS retransmission of Section 7.1 as a new flight mail, never by a reading of the text part. An intermediary that drops the typed part from every flight ends every attempt through it: this carriage does not pass such an intermediary, and says so rather than pretending the text part is a fallback.

section.name: Size gates
section.t: A flight mail is subject to the version 1 size cap for mail on this binding, and that cap applies 1st: a receiver MUST refuse a flight mail whose raw object exceeds the cap before it decodes any base64, allocates any reassembly state, or feeds any octet to a DTLS stack.

Within the carriage, a datagram MUST NOT exceed the carriage datagram limit. The reference implementation's limit is 262144 octets, and its default chunk is 32768 base64 characters (24576 decoded octets at most per part before the header). Both are local limits, configurable within the bounds of Sections 6 and 16.4; a sender that does not know the receiver's limits SHOULD keep a datagram within the reference limit. A part count MUST NOT exceed 1024.

section.name: Segmentation and Reassembly
section.t: A sender segments a datagram when its base64 form exceeds 1 chunk. Every part of 1 transfer carries the same transfer identifier, part count, byte count, and digest, and a distinct index. A sender MUST NOT place parts of 2 datagrams in 1 flight mail, and MUST NOT place any datagram octets in a mail whose subject is not a flight subject.
The receiver's reassembly state is keyed by (mail session-id, transfer identifier). Its rules are:

li.t: Parts MAY arrive in any order. Duplicate parts are idempotent: the same index with the same chunk changes nothing.

A part that contradicts its transfer -- a different chunk for an index already held, or different header fields for the transfer -- destroys the transfer. The receiver drops the state and completes nothing from it. The sender may start the transfer again under a new transfer identifier.

A transfer completes when every index is held and the concatenated datagram matches the declared byte count and digest. A completed datagram is delivered upward exactly once, and the state is discarded.

Incomplete state is bounded in count, in total size, and in age, and expires. The reference implementation holds at most 64 transfers. A transfer's age runs from its FIRST part as well as its last: the reference implementation keeps a transfer for at most 3600 seconds from its first part, and 3600 seconds from its last part, and no arriving part extends the first-part deadline -- a sender dripping 1 part just inside the idle window would otherwise hold a transfer slot indefinitely. Expired parts complete nothing: a part that arrives after its transfer expired starts a new, incomplete transfer.

section.t: Reassembly is deliberately unauthenticated and therefore deliberately cheap to discard: it holds bytes, it decides nothing, and the first decision any reassembled datagram faces is the DTLS stack's.

section.name: Retransmission is DTLS's
section.t: The carriage defines no acknowledgement and no retransmission timer of its own. Retransmission is the DTLS handshake's, as version 1's profile inherits it from : each side re-sends its current flight when its timer expires, and the timers' values are the profile's. On this carriage a flight's re-send is a new flight mail, under a new transfer identifier. The re-sent flight is the DTLS stack's own retransmission -- from the record layer's perspective a new record, with a new record sequence number ( Section 5.2) -- not a copy of the earlier mail. A sender SHOULD NOT re-send a flight mail at the mail layer on its own schedule: 2 retransmission machines on 1 path multiply mail without adding reliability.

Timers that are reasonable on a live path are short on a store-and-forward one. An implementation on this carriage SHOULD stretch its retransmission timers toward the mailbox poll rhythm it operates on: concretely, the initial retransmission interval SHOULD be at least 2 of the implementation's mailbox poll periods, and an attempt SHOULD be given up after about 8 retransmissions -- that give-up is the attempt deadline of Section 9.4. Section 5.8.2 permits a profile to recommend longer timer values than its defaults; this paragraph is that recommendation for a store-and-forward path. Stretching a timer changes no message and no state machine; it is a local matter.

section.name: Duplicates, at each layer
section.t: Mail is delivered at least once by some hops and exactly observed twice by some pollers; DTLS is written for a network that duplicates datagrams; and the job layer is written to run each job at most once. The carriage keeps the 3 layers' duplicate handling separate, and each layer's rule is its own:

li.t: Mail layer: the carriage suppresses exact duplicates, split by phase. A receiver keeps a digest of each datagram it has accepted from flight mail, bounded and in arrival order; the reference implementation's cache holds 4096 digests, evicting the least recently seen (a hit refreshes an entry's place). The cache is an optimization against a poller or a sender delivering the same mail twice; it is not the replay defense (Section 13 names the defenses). The connection-id binding check of Section 9.2 runs before a datagram's digest is recorded, so a misaddressed copy cannot poison the cache against the same record arriving under its own session's mail. A digest hit on a handshake-phase datagram is not fed to the DTLS stack again -- nothing is derived twice -- and the receiver instead re-posts its saved last outbound flight, under a new transfer identifier: the duplicate is the signal that the answer was lost ( Section 5.8.1). The re-post is budgeted, because on this carriage it costs an outbound mail that an unauthenticated sender can provoke with a captured hello: a receiver MUST re-post a saved flight at most once per generation of that flight. A digest hit spends the 1 re-post the saved flight carries; only a new flight from the DTLS stack -- a new answer, or the stack's own retransmission on its timer -- arms another; further bit-identical copies of a handshake-phase datagram are dropped. A thousand copies of 1 ClientHello therefore cost the responder at most 1 HelloRetryRequest mail beyond the 1 it already sent (Section 16.4). A digest hit on application data is dropped and does nothing. A replayed mail is therefore not a new record at either layer, and a lost flight is still repaired. A retransmission under Section 5.2 is not this case. It is a new record, with a new record sequence number, carrying the same handshake message, so it is not bit-identical to the datagram already accepted. It misses this cache, enters the stack, and is answered by the stack. The budget does not limit it, and if the single re-post was itself lost, that retransmission is what repairs the attempt.

DTLS layer: records are protected and sequenced by the record layer as specifies; a record that does not authenticate is dropped by the stack, whether it is a forgery, a corruption, or a replay the mail layer did not catch.
Job layer: a job inside a session faces the version 1 acceptance gate, whose seen-set runs it at most once (Section 10.2), under the same priced replay windows as any other binding.

section.t: A duplicate flight mail MUST NOT create a 2nd session, MUST NOT deliver an application message twice, and MUST NOT cause a job to run twice. A duplicate part MUST NOT complete a transfer twice.

section.name: Ordering
section.t: No ordering is assumed anywhere in this carriage. Flight mails of 1 attempt can arrive in any order; the handshake state machines of already tolerate reordered flights, and parts tolerate reordering under Section 6. Application messages inside a session keep the session's own order, which the record layer defines; the order in which different jobs' mails reached the mailbox is not an input to anything.

section.name: The Mailbox Parser: Lane Dispatch and Recognition
Dispatch order
section.t: On a runner that has enabled this carriage, the mailbox parser classifies each message it fetches before anything is delivered anywhere. The classification is by subject grammar and body shape, in this order:

li.t: A message whose subject matches the flight subject is DTLS input. It goes to the carriage, and to nothing else. The unaddressed harness subject is not this case on a deployment mailbox: it is malformed flight mail (Section 5.1) and is not fed to a DTLS stack.
A message whose subject is a version 1 job subject is a job for the acceptance gate, as before.
Everything else is other mail, handled as before.

section.t: DTLS classification happens in the component that owns the mailbox (in the reference implementation, the email transport extension), because that is where the DTLS server for this carriage runs (Section 4.3). The runner core -- the acceptance gate -- never sees flight mail.

section.name: Recognizing the initialization flight
section.t: A complete datagram is an initialization flight when its 1st record is a plaintext handshake record whose handshake message is one complete ClientHello. A fragmented or incomplete first handshake message is not an initialization. It is malformed flight mail: consumed, dropped, not answered, and allocated no reassembly state. The profile's ClientHello is one message, and this carriage does not reassemble handshake fragments before a cookie has validated. A complete datagram that parses as DTLS records but is not an initialization is a session datagram. The recognition is of the DTLS bytes, not of the subject: the subject routes a message to the carriage, and the bytes decide what the carriage does with it.

An initialization flight is answered as version 1's profile answers it: statelessly, with a HelloRetryRequest, before any session state exists. A first flight that is not a complete ClientHello draws no HelloRetryRequest.

section.name: Fail closed
section.t: A message with a DTLS subject whose body does not frame a datagram under Section 5.2, whose session-id is not a valid session-id, whose declared sizes are out of range, whose digest does not match a completed datagram, or whose datagram is not a DTLS record at all, is malformed flight mail. It is:

li.t: consumed as DTLS input -- marked seen, so it is not offered again on every poll; and
dropped -- it produces no session, no application message, no job, and no result; and
never reinterpreted as a job or as any other kind of mail.

section.t: An implementation MUST NOT fall back from a DTLS-shaped failure to any other reading of the same message. The lane a message enters by its subject is the only lane it is ever read in.

section.name: Seen flags and fetches
section.t: Flight mail is consumed by the component that owns the mailbox, and consumption is what marks it seen. A party MUST mark a flight message seen only when it has consumed it -- fed it to the carriage, or determined it malformed under Section 8.3. A fetch made to decide, before consumption, MUST NOT set the seen flag: over IMAP that is a BODY.PEEK fetch, because a plain body fetch sets the flag as a side effect, and a fetcher that marks its peer's flights seen starves every other consumer of the same mailbox. An initiator MUST ignore flight mail whose mail session-id is not an attempt it has open: on a shared mailbox, stale flights of dead attempts are normal, and they are not input.

section.name: The attempt, flight by flight
section.t: An attempt proceeds exactly as the datagram binding's handshake, with mail as the datagram path:

li.t: The initiator sends its ClientHello as flight mail under a fresh mail session-id.
The responder, stateless, answers with a HelloRetryRequest flight mail under the same mail session-id.
The initiator answers with its cookied ClientHello.

The responder validates the cookie and the PSK binder, derives the handshake keys from the ephemeral exchange, and sends its flight: ServerHello, EncryptedExtensions (carrying the platform disclosure, Section 11), and Finished.
The initiator verifies the flight, holds the disclosure (Section 11), and sends its Finished. The session is established at both ends when the responder verifies that Finished.

section.t: No step of this exchange is a job, produces a job, or is visible to the acceptance gate.

section.name: Identity binding at establishment
section.t: The responder's DTLS core needs a peer address to bind its cookie and its session to. On the datagram binding that is the datagram's source address. On this carriage there is no source address a receiver may trust: the From header is a claim any sender can write, and the mailbox's identifiers are local to the mailbox. The peer address on this carriage is the ASCII string email: followed by the mail session-id. That string is an untrusted routing label: it demultiplexes concurrent attempts on 1 mailbox, and it is not a credential, not a mailbox identity, and not a key selector. The cookie key is a secret of the responder, generated by the responder and not derived from the address or from anything the message asserts, so binding the cookie to an attacker-chosen label is safe exactly while that key stays secret. The key's lifetime is the matter of Section 9.4. The PSK identity inside the handshake selects the shared secret, including any additional secret, exactly as version 1 specifies; the mail session-id never selects a key.
When a session establishes, the carriage binds the mail session-id to the session's connection ID. From then on:

li.t: A protected record is accepted under a mail session-id only if its destination connection ID is the connection ID bound to that mail session-id.
A record whose connection ID is bound to a different mail session-id is dropped, whichever subject it arrived under.

section.t: A record therefore cannot be moved from 1 session to another by relabeling its mail, and a session cannot be entered by naming it: entry is the record protection itself, which only the session's keys satisfy.

section.name: Resumption
section.t: Resumption over this carriage follows the profile: tickets MAY be issued and, on this carriage, MUST be single-use. A ticket is stored mail like any other flight, in the same archive as the transcript, and a replayed ticket MUST NOT become a second long-lived secret. (Version 1's SHOULD for the datagram binding is unchanged.) A resumed handshake is a full handshake in everything that matters here -- a fresh mail session-id, a fresh ephemeral share, psk_dhe_ke only, and a fresh platform disclosure (Section 11). A deployment MAY disable resumption on this carriage by configuration; doing so changes no message, only how often full handshakes happen.

section.name: Attempt deadline and failure
section.t: An attempt that cannot complete -- a flight that never comes, a binder that never verifies, a peer that stops answering -- is abandoned by the side waiting on it when its retransmission gives up, and its partial state (reassembly state, digest cache entries, the mail session-id binding) expires with the bounds of Sections 6 and 7.2. A failed attempt leaves the ordinary email binding untouched and has no effect on any other attempt.

The cookie key of Section 9.2 has a lifetime this path tests and the datagram path never did. On the datagram binding a HelloRetryRequest is answered within a round trip, inside 1 process lifetime of the responder. On this carriage it is answered on a later poll -- an hour later on a slow poller -- which may be after the responder's process has restarted. A responder SHOULD keep its cookie key across its own restarts for at least the attempt deadline, kept as the shared secret is kept: in the responder's own state, never in a flight, and never derived from the address or from anything a message asserts (Section 9.2). The reference implementation keeps it beside the mailbox's own state, readable by its owner only. A responder whose cookie key does not survive a restart abandons every attempt in flight at that restart: the cookied ClientHello fails the cookie check and is ignored, each retransmission of it fails the same way, and the initiator abandons the attempt when its retransmission gives up. Recovery is a fresh attempt under a new mail session-id, never a repair of the old one. Established sessions do not survive a restart of either end on any binding -- their keys are erased with the process, as Section 16.1 requires -- and a result held for such a session follows Section 10.3.

section.name: Session end
section.t: A session ends by alert, by the profile's own mechanisms, or by being forgotten: a store-and-forward peer can vanish without a farewell, and an implementation MUST NOT keep a session's keys, or its mail session-id binding, past the session's configured lifetime. Keys are erased with the session (Section 16.1). A result that is waiting for a dead session is not sent on any other path (Section 12); it is held under Section 10.3's bounds and expires under them -- it is not kept forever, and expiry never sends it.

section.name: Jobs and Results Inside a Session
Framing
section.t: Application data on the session is framed as version 1's session profile frames it: a 4-octet big-endian length prefix per message, and each application message is exactly 1 envelope -- the subject line, a blank line, and the object body -- in the shape the version 1 channel envelope uses. A job travels as the envelope of its job object. A result travels as the envelope of its result object.

On the runner, a completed application message is converted back into that ordinary envelope and delivered to the runner core through the same channel an ordinary mail job crosses. The core cannot tell, and does not need to tell, that the envelope arrived inside a session.

The objects are version 1 objects. A job inside a session is a version 1 job object and a result inside a session is a version 1 result object, with the version value version 1 defines; the 3 of this document numbers the document and its carriage only, and no object in a session carries it.

section.name: The acceptance gate, in full, inside the session
section.t: Completing a DTLS handshake MUST NOT bypass, widen, or substitute for the job acceptance gate. A job carried inside a session is admitted exactly as the same job arriving as ordinary mail: it needs its valid HMAC signature under the shared secret, its correct audience, and its compliance with the size caps (the whole-job cap, the script cap, and the envelope cap of version 1), and it is refused on the same terms -- staleness, key policy, and the rest of version 1 Section 14's checks -- as any other job.

The session authenticates the channel; the signature authenticates the object. Neither stands in for the other, and the version 1 rule stands verbatim on this carriage: a cleartext object inside a session is still refused unless the operator has enabled cleartext acceptance, because the session's confidentiality is not the object's provenance.

The 2 keys are checked independently. The PSK identity that opened the session and the key id that signed a job inside it need not name the same key: the gate reads the job's own key id and applies that key's policy, and the session's key confers nothing on the job and takes nothing from it. A job signed under 1 key MAY be carried by a session opened under another, exactly as a signed job may be carried by any mailbox. An implementation MUST NOT admit, widen, or narrow a job on the strength of the PSK identity of the session that carried it: the session does not authorize the job, and the job does not authorize the session. (The session's key does decide 1 thing, which is not admission: where the job's result may go, Section 10.3.)

section.name: Results are session-bound
section.t: A result for a job that arrived inside a session is sent inside that session, sealed as application data. The carriage remembers, for each job it delivered from a session, the session's connection ID and the job ident together, and the PSK identity the session authenticated under -- never the job ident alone, which the submitter chooses and which collides across submitters. The hold is kept as the result is kept, in the responder's own state and across a restart of the process. A hold that died with the process would send the result by the ordinary path on the next pass, which Section 12 forbids. If that session no longer exists when the result is ready, the result waits, and it can still leave on this carriage in exactly 1 way: inside a later session that authenticated under the same PSK identity and that carries the same job ident again. The acceptance gate refuses the repeated job as a replay (Section 13); the held result is what answers it. A job whose ident is held for another PSK identity's job is not delivered: it is logged and dropped, because the hold belongs to the submitter whose job it was, and delivering it would put that submitter's result, or that submitter's job file, in the wrong hands. A held result MUST NOT be sent as an ordinary mail result, MUST NOT be sent inside a session under a different PSK identity, and MUST NOT be sent inside a different job's session as if it were that job's. Section 12 states the general rule this follows from.

The PSK identity distinguishes submitters only as finely as the key directory. Two peers that authenticate with the same secret are the same identity, and a later session of that identity which carries the job ident again is a legitimate destination for the held result. Distinct submitters are distinct keys, which version 1's additional secrets already are. This carriage does not invent a finer name for a submitter, and a mail session-id is not one: the initiator chooses it, and a resumption uses a fresh one (Section 9.3).

The hold is bounded, as the hold of any state on this carriage is bounded. A held result expires by age -- the reference implementation's bound is 7 days -- and the held set as a whole is bounded in count and in total bytes, oldest first. An expired result is dropped and the expiry is logged; it is never sent. Dropping is not downgrade: downgrade would be sending the result by a weaker path.

section.name: Platform Disclosure on This Carriage
section.t: The platform disclosure is the version 1 Section 20 mechanism, unchanged: the initiator offers the platform_info extension, empty, in its ClientHello; the responder MAY answer with a disclosure object, and answers only in EncryptedExtensions; it MUST NOT send the disclosure unsolicited or in any other message; the tiers are version 1's (none, family by default, standard, full); the initiator cannot ask for a wider tier; and a resumed session carries the disclosure again.

The carriage is why the mechanism matters most here. On a live path, a post-handshake greeting costs a round trip of milliseconds. Over a mailbox, it costs a poll cycle at best and a day of latency at worst -- and for a submitter that plans work from the platform card, it costs that on every session, before any work can be planned against the platform it is about to address. Riding the final handshake flight -- the pattern version 1 lifts from IKEv2's Configuration Payload , Section 3.15 -- means the initiator holds the platform at the moment the session is established, having sent and received exactly the flights the handshake already needed. Even a rudimentary exchange counts: a responder that can say only its disclosure tier and its operating system family has still saved the round trip.

The precondition that makes the early disclosure acceptable is stated here, not left to the flight order alone: the responder sends EncryptedExtensions only in a flight it builds after the cookie has validated and the PSK binder has verified (Section 9.1, step 4). A peer that does not hold the shared secret cannot produce a verifying binder, and never receives the disclosure; an unauthenticated ClientHello is not enough to extract a platform card. The accepted cost of version 1 Section 20 stands on this carriage too: the disclosure is made a half-step earlier than a post-handshake mechanism would make it, before the responder has verified the initiator's Finished. Version 1's security considerations argue the point; this document adopts the argument.

section.name: No-Downgrade Rules
section.t: The following are stated in 1 place because downgrade is the failure this carriage is most often suspected of, and each rule already exists somewhere above or in version 1:

li.t: psk_ke MUST NOT be offered, accepted, or fallen back to, on this carriage or any other (Section 4.1). A peer that offers only psk_ke gets no session.

A session's keys are never a fallback for the object crypto, and the object crypto is never a fallback for a session: a job that was to travel inside a session does not travel as an ordinary encrypted mail job instead when the session fails (Section 10.2's gate is the same, but the carriage of the object is part of what the submitter chose).
A cleartext object inside a session is refused on the version 1 terms (Section 10.2). DTLS carriage is not a way to make cleartext acceptable.
A result bound to a session is never downgraded to an ordinary mail result (Sections 10.3 and 12).
Flight mail that fails is never reinterpreted as a job (Section 8.3). There is no reading of a message under which a failed handshake becomes work.

The mail hop's own TLS (Section 16.2) is never a substitute for the session: a deployment MUST NOT accept "the mailbox connection was encrypted" as a reason to run a session-less job with session-level trust.

section.name: Replay Handling
section.t: Replay is handled at 3 layers, each in its own terms, and no layer is asked to do another's work:

li.t: A replayed flight mail meets the mail layer's rule, split by phase (Section 7.2): a handshake-phase replay re-posts the saved flight without re-entering the stack -- once per generation of that flight, and then it is dropped -- and an application-data replay is dropped before it. A replayed initialization therefore cannot create a duplicate session: at worst, a replay that evades the cache meets the cookie exchange and the handshake state machine, which answer a retransmitted ClientHello with the flight it already produced and derive nothing twice. Early data has no layer here at all: a ClientHello carrying early data is rejected as a malformed flight (Section 4.1), and this profile derives no epoch-1 keys for a replay to use. is the reason the rule is a rejection and not a quiet skip: 0-RTT data is not forward secret, is replayable between connections, and an application protocol must not use it without a profile that says how ( Sections 2.3 and 8, Appendix F.5). A job that runs a program is not safe to replay, and on a mailbox the ClientHello can sit for a day.

A replayed record meets the record layer: sequence numbers and AEAD verification under decide, and a record that does not verify is dropped. A replayed application message that somehow reached the core would meet the job layer next in any case.

A replayed job meets the acceptance gate's seen-set: at most once, with the 2 priced windows version 1 documents (a crash between run and result, and the seen record ageing out), and no 3rd window is opened by this carriage -- the carriage adds no execution path, so it adds no replay path to execution.

section.t: Resumption tickets on this carriage MUST be single-use (Section 9.3); version 1's SHOULD stands for the datagram binding. A replayed ticket can at most restart a handshake that still demands fresh ephemeral keys and a fresh binder under the ticket's key.

section.name: Operational Considerations
section.t: The carriage shares the mailbox with the ordinary email binding. Flight mail and job mail are distinguished by the parser's dispatch (Section 8.1) and neither delays the other beyond 1 poll pass; an operator enables the carriage per runner, and disabling it returns the mailbox to exactly its previous behavior, with any in-flight attempts expiring under Section 9.4.

Poll rhythm is the operational dial that matters. A runner that polls its mailbox every 20 seconds completes a handshake in about 4 poll cycles when both sides are prompt; a runner that polls hourly completes it in about 4 hours. Nothing in the protocol changes -- only the timers an implementation should choose (Section 7.1) and the patience of the submitter. Operators pairing this carriage with a slow poll SHOULD say so in the platform card's customary ways, so a submitter can tell a slow session from a dead one.

Sessions are state, and state on a store-and-forward path should be visible to the operator: an implementation SHOULD log session establishment, abandonment, and expiry, and the dropping of malformed flight mail, at the same verbosity it logs refused jobs. It MUST NOT log session keys, ephemeral material, or the shared secret, on this carriage or any other.

section.name: IANA Considerations
section.t: This document requests no IANA action.

The platform_info extension's code point is version 1's IANA action, stated in version 1 Section 18: a value in the TLS ExtensionType Values registry, TBD there, with 0xFFA0 in interim private use. This document reuses that extension exactly as version 1 defines it, on a new carriage; it does not request a 2nd value, a new registry, a port, a service name, a media type, or an OID. The DTLS reference port 20220 remains version 1's local default for the datagram binding and is not used by this carriage.

The carriage's MIME content type (Section 5.2) is an unregistered name in the standards tree, used by a local draft; this document requests no media type registration for it. A future standards-track revision is where such a request would belong.
As a local, unsubmitted draft, this document could not ground an assignment in any case: nothing in it is to be read as requesting that IANA act, early or otherwise.

section.name: Perfect forward secrecy
section.t: The property this version exists for: a session's keys are derived from an ephemeral exchange performed fresh in that session's handshake -- X25519, or the hybrid exchange of Section 4.4 -- combined with the pre-shared key (Section 4.1), and are erased when the session ends. The shared secret authenticates; it does not encrypt the session.

It follows that recording every flight mail of a session -- and mail is recorded by design: it is stored by the sender's provider, the receiver's provider, and the mailbox itself -- and later obtaining the shared secret does not decrypt the session. The recorded flights are a ClientHello, a HelloRetryRequest, a cookied ClientHello, a server flight, a Finished, and protected records. Without the ephemeral private keys, which never leave the endpoints and do not survive the session, the protected records stay protected.

The limits of the property are the usual ones, and are stated plainly: compromise of the shared secret permits impersonation in future handshakes and an active man-in-the-middle of a future session, because the PSK is the authentication; it permits reading ordinary version 1 mail jobs that rely on the object crypto, which is why this carriage exists; and it does nothing for an endpoint that is itself compromised while a session is live. Forward secrecy is a property of recorded sessions against later key compromise, and that is the property claimed -- no more, and no less.

One further limit belongs to this carriage in particular, because mail is archived by design. Where the ephemeral exchange is the bare X25519 -- the ephemeral exchange tells operators to prefer, and the right choice against the adversary above -- a party that records a session's flights (and on this carriage the sender's provider, the receiver's provider, and the mailbox all hold them) and that later breaks X25519, by whatever means, decrypts the recorded session without ever learning the shared secret. Forward secrecy there is secrecy against later compromise of the long-term secret; it is not secrecy against a later break of the ephemeral's algorithm.

The remedy is the hybrid share of Section 4.4, X25519MLKEM768 , and it is part of this profile, not a shape reserved for a later revision: the reference implementation implements it, and a session on this carriage negotiates it whenever both endpoints offer it. In a hybrid session the ephemeral secret is the ML-KEM secret and the X25519 secret together, so the limit above narrows to the sessions that negotiated the bare share: a later break of X25519 alone does not decrypt a hybrid session, and neither does a later break of ML-KEM alone; the recorded session falls only if both halves fall, or the endpoint itself does. The psk_dhe_ke rule is unchanged -- the PSK still only authenticates, the ephemeral share, bare or hybrid, is what encrypts, and TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384 remains the suite.

section.name: The mailbox as intermediary
section.t: On this carriage the mailbox provider, and any hop that stores flight mail, holds the session's whole transcript in the clear at the DTLS-record layer: subjects, sizes, timing, counts, and the handshake's public values are visible to it, and protected records are visible as ciphertext. The provider cannot read application data, cannot forge a record that verifies, and cannot complete a handshake, not holding the shared secret. It can delay, drop, duplicate, and reorder mail; Sections 7 and 13 are written so that each of those is survivable and none is profitable. Deployments that care about the metadata itself should note that the mail session-id, the flight cadence, and datagram sizes are all observable; this document specifies no padding or cover traffic.

section.name: Headers are not authentication
section.t: Every routing decision in this carriage is made from untrusted text -- the subject -- and every authentication decision is made from protected bytes. The synthetic peer address of Section 9.2 exists precisely so that no spoofable header becomes a security input: a flight mail that claims any From whatsoever is treated identically, and is worth exactly what its datagram proves. A deployment MUST NOT add a sender allowlist as a substitute gate on this carriage; the version 1 properties already record that the email binding carries no sender gate and claims none.

section.name: Pre-authentication resource bounds
section.t: Everything a receiver does before a binder verifies is a resource an unauthenticated sender can spend, so the pre-authentication surface is bounded at each step, and each action such a sender can cause is listed here with the number that bounds it:

li.t: A fresh ClientHello costs the responder 1 HelloRetryRequest mail and no session state: the cookie exchange keeps the responder stateless until a cookie validates (Section 4.1). That is 1 small mail out for 1 mail in -- the price of a stateless responder on any binding, with no amplification.

A bit-identical copy of a handshake-phase flight costs at most 1 re-post of the saved flight per generation of that flight (Section 7.2), so a captured hello is worth at most 1 extra outbound mail and never a mail per copy.
A flight mail is refused above the mail size cap before any decoding (Section 5.3).

A reassembly slot is 1 of at most 64, bounded in total size, and held at most 3600 seconds from its first part and from its last; a contradiction destroys the transfer rather than arbitrating it (Section 6).
A digest-cache entry is 1 of 4096, the least recently seen evicted first (Section 7.2).

A saved outbound flight is 1 of 4096, first in first out, the same bound as the digest cache. Evicting one drops only the spare re-post for that peer. A retransmission is a new record and is answered by the stack without the saved flight (Section 7.2).

A malformed flight is consumed in 1 pass and 1 log line, not re-offered on every poll (Section 8.3). A fragmented or incomplete first handshake message is this case: it draws no HelloRetryRequest and no reassembly state (Section 8.2).
The unaddressed harness subject, on a deployment mailbox, is this case too: consumed, not fed to a DTLS stack, and worth no answer (Section 5.1).

section.t: An action an unauthenticated sender can cause that has no number in this list is a defect in this document. The platform disclosure's cost -- disclosure before the initiator's Finished is verified -- is inherited from version 1 Section 20 and bounded by its tiers; a responder that discloses at the none or family tier spends little on an unauthenticated peer, and the choice of tier is the responder's.

section.name: Downgrade and substitution
section.t: Section 12 collects the no-downgrade rules. The general statement behind them: at no point does this carriage answer a failure by doing the same thing more weakly. A failed handshake is a failed handshake; a dead session holds its results; a malformed flight is dropped. An implementation that adds a fallback -- plain job crypto for a session's job, ordinary mail for a session's result, a job reading for a flight's bytes -- has left this specification, and should expect the security properties of Sections 16.1 and 10.2 to leave with it.

section.name: The gate is the security boundary for execution
section.t: It is worth restating the architecture once, because the carriage can make it look otherwise: DTLS authenticates a channel between holders of the shared secret, of which there may be several (version 1's additional secrets and key policies distinguish them). The acceptance gate -- signature, audience, caps, key policy, seen-set -- is what decides whether a job runs, whose it is, and whether it has run before. Carrying a job inside a session changes the confidentiality and integrity of its transport and adds forward secrecy; it changes its admission not at all. Any future extension of this carriage that proposes to admit a job on the session's authority alone is proposing to remove the gate, and should be reviewed as such.

The constraint that narrows what a session may cause is the key policy of the key that signs the job, which is version 1's and is unchanged here. A deployment that wants one key to run only a pinned script states that on the key: the kinds it may name, the interpreters it may name, and the digest of the script it may carry. The session does not widen that policy, and the policy does not depend on this carriage. A holder of a different key, or of only the traffic keys of the session, does not inherit it. The gate reads the job's own key and applies that key's policy (Section 10.2).
